name: Mascara / waterproof mascara
lead: Mascara is a cosmetic applied to the eyelashes to darken, thicken, lengthen and define them. A pigmented coat makes the lashes contrast more with the skin and the white of the eye, so the eyes look larger and the eye area more defined. It is most often a liquid in a tube with a brush, and formulas combine pigments, oils, waxes and preservatives [1][2].

Waterproof mascara is a variant built from hydrophobic ingredients so that it resists water, sweat and tears. People choose it for swimming, humid weather, long days or events where a standard formula would smudge, and they typically remove it with an oil-based remover [1][3]. Tubing mascaras are a related category in which film-forming polymers wrap each lash and come off with warm water [1].

The cultural history runs from kohl in ancient Egypt, worn by men and women, through the 19th-century petroleum-jelly formulas of Eugene Rimmel and the early 20th-century Maybelline business, to the 1935 patent for a waterproof cream mascara [1][14][15]. A 2011 review in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery notes that long, dark lashes and prominent eyes are often associated with attractiveness, confidence and well-being, and lists mascara as the temporary option next to artificial lashes, transplantation and prostaglandin-based products [8].

In looksmaxxing communities, some male users discuss mascara, especially on the lower lashes, as a low-cost way to make the eye area look more defined, usually alongside concern about the result being noticed [3]. Reported risks include allergic reactions, styes, eyelid swelling and contamination of old product; waterproof products had the highest rate of detected organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in a 2021 survey of cosmetics [1]. No clinical trials of mascara as a looks intervention have been published.

paras: Mascara coats lash hairs with pigment and conditioning ingredients to make them appear darker and fuller, and the effect is temporary. Formulations contain pigments, oils and waxes; iron oxides (black, brown, red and yellow) and titanium dioxide are the most common pigments, and some products add ultramarine blue. Oils such as linseed, castor and lanolin and waxes such as paraffin, carnauba and beeswax give the product its texture, and conditioners such as panthenol are sometimes added.[1]

Formats are broadly liquid, cream or powder, with liquid in a tube and brush the most common. Tubing mascaras use film-forming polymers that wrap individual lashes, and products sold to lengthen or curl often include nylon or rayon microfibres.[1] Water-resistant mascaras use hydrophobic ingredients such as dodecane, while non-waterproof versions use water-soluble bases.[1]

Eye darkening with kohl is documented in ancient Egypt, with Wikipedia citing use by all social classes from about 3100 BCE and the Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) describing its compounds as protective for the eyes. Kohl was traditionally made by crushing stibnite, and later formulations often used galena (lead sulfide) [14]. A painting from the tomb of Nakht in Thebes (15th century BC) shows both men and women wearing eye makeup [16]. Victorian-era women made mascara at home by heating ash or lampblack with elderberry juice [1].

In the 19th century the perfumer Eugene Rimmel developed a petroleum jelly-based product, and his name became a generic word for mascara in several languages [1]. In 1915 the Chicago pharmacist Thomas Lyle Williams made a similar mixture for his sister Mabel, sold locally as Lash-Brow-Ine; in 1917 it became Maybelline Cake Mascara, described as the first modern eye cosmetic for everyday use [1][15]. Cake mascara was applied by rubbing a dampened brush on a cake of soap and black dye, which remained messy [1]. Williams sold the company to Plough (later Schering-Plough) in 1967, and L'Oreal acquired Maybelline in 1996 [15].
After World War I, the rival entrepreneurs Elizabeth Arden and Helena Rubinstein launched mascara lines, and film stars such as Theda Bara, Greta Garbo and Jean Harlow popularised the look [1].

Helene Winterstein-Kambersky, a Viennese opera singer, patented a waterproof cream mascara in 1935, and Rubinstein licensed the recipe about four years later [1]. Rubinstein introduced a lotion-based tube-and-brush product in 1957 and the refillable Mascara Matic tube in 1958; Max Factor's waterproof liquid tube mascara dates from 1960 according to the images in Wikipedia's article [1]. Grokipedia's account differs on some of these dates, attributing the pioneering of waterproof mascara to Rubinstein in 1938 [2]. A grooved applicator rod was later replaced by the brush now used [1].

A 2026 narrative review in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery traces the cultural meaning of long lashes from ancient Greece, where they were linked to restraint and modesty, to modern cosmetics, lash serums and transplantation, and notes that on digital platforms exaggerated lashes now signify youth and desirability [9].

Among the male forum users who mention it, the lower lashes are the usual target [3]. Formulas are chosen by effect: lengthening products contain nylon or rayon microfibres, curling and tubing products use polymers, and waterproof products are picked where moisture is expected [1]. Waterproof types resist ordinary cleansing and are typically taken off with an oil-based remover; a looksmax.org poster reports that a waterproof product needed coconut oil and several minutes to remove [3]. A shelf life of two to four months once opened is cited, because lashes naturally carry microbes that can contaminate the tube [1][7].

Wikipedia's mascara article does not cover male use and refers readers to a separate page on male cosmetics [1]. Its eyeliner coverage records that Egyptian men wore kohl in antiquity and that the term 'guyliner' was popularised in the early 2000s by emo-scene musicians in bands such as Fall Out Boy and Panic! at the Disco [16]. In looksmaxxing forums, male users who describe trying mascara typically treat it as a subtle, situational tool for the lower lashes rather than a daily look, and often ask whether others can tell they are wearing it [3][6].

Wikipedia reports that styes and swollen eyelids from allergic reactions are more common than toxic effects, with methylparaben, aluminum powder, ceteareth-20, butylparaben and benzyl alcohol among reported triggers. Mascara can also incubate microbes because lashes naturally carry them, and the FDA's stated shelf life is two to four months. Improperly cleaned product can deposit under the conjunctiva as black lumps.[1][10] A review of contact dermatitis to cosmetics covers allergic reactions to cosmetic ingredients generally.[4]

A pilot randomised study of 40 women aged 18 to 39 investigated microbial contamination of two brands of non-waterproof mascara used daily for three months, examining whether application inoculates the tube with microbes from the lashes.[7] Case reports in Ophthalmology (subconjunctival mascara deposition) and Clinical and Experimental Dermatology document mascara-related eye and skin findings, and a 1991 review lists mascara among factors associated with Pseudomonas corneal ulcers.[10][11][12]

The 1933 Lash Lure product, which contained para-phenylenediamine, was followed by blindness in about sixteen women and one death from infection; the US gave the FDA authority over cosmetics in 1938.[1] Kohl-type products such as kajal and surma often carry a lead poisoning risk and are described as illegal color additives in the United States.[1] Thiomersal, a mercury compound, has been used as a preservative, and in 2008 Minnesota became the first US state to ban intentionally added mercury in cosmetics.[1]

A 2021 study of 231 makeup and personal care products found organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in over half; waterproof mascara had the highest rate, at 82 percent of brands tested, and manufacturers often do not label PFAS content.[1] A study of 100 Latina adolescents found that daily makeup users had higher urinary levels of some phthalates, parabens and phenols than rare users, though that study was not specific to mascara.[5]

Regulators have begun to act on PFAS in cosmetics. California's Toxic-Free Cosmetics Act, which bans intentionally added PFAS, took effect on 1 January 2025, and France's ban took effect on 20 February 2025, according to Grokipedia, which also reports a 2014 study of 100 women linking long-term mascara use with lash loss in 19 percent of long-term users, with causation not established [2]. The FDA's cosmetics authority itself dates to the 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, passed after the Lash Lure incident [1].

On looksmax.org, some users post about trying mascara on the lower lashes or the eye area to make the eyes look more defined. One poster wrote that darkening the lash lines made the area look better and that the bottom row made the biggest difference, while the main drawback was avoiding being noticed; the same poster reported that a waterproof product needed coconut oil and several minutes to remove.[3] Others in the thread suggested castor oil on lashes as an option they considered less obviously cosmetic.[3] Other threads show users posting photos or video wearing mascara and asking for opinions.[6]

Wikipedia's mascara article does not cover male use and refers readers to a separate page on male cosmetics.[1] Male grooming more broadly is discussed in the same communities alongside skin care, brow grooming and eyelash-growth products.

The 2011 review describes other ways of enhancing lashes: artificial lashes adhered to the lid margin or to individual lashes, eyelash transplantation, and over-the-counter lash products, some of which contain prostaglandin analogues whose safety and efficacy have not been fully studied. It also notes that bimatoprost, originally an eye-pressure drug, was approved for hypotrichosis of the eyelashes.[8]

No studies found of mascara as an appearance intervention. Related research includes cosmetics-safety work such as the PFAS survey and the urinary biomarker study noted above, the pilot study of microbial contamination in mascara used for three months, and a 2020 laboratory formulation study of a curling mascara with a thermoresponsive polymer.[1][5][7][13]

lore.intro: Mascara appears in looksmaxxing discussion as a low-cost way to define the eye area, with users commenting on the visibility of the result and on whether it is socially noticeable.[3][6]

claims.claim: Mascara on the lower lashes makes the eye area look more defined
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster says darkening the lash lines made the eye area look better, with the lower lashes making the biggest difference, and that the main problem was avoiding being noticed.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined mascara's effect on attractiveness in men. Reference sources describe its purpose as darkening, thickening and defining lashes, and a 2011 review notes that long, dark lashes are often associated with attractiveness.[1][8]

claims.claim: Waterproof mascara is hard to remove without oil
claims.believers: A poster reports that a waterproof product needed oil such as coconut oil to remove and took several minutes.[3]
claims.experts: Waterproof formulas use hydrophobic ingredients that resist water, which is consistent with the report.[1]

claims.claim: Castor oil on the lashes is a more discreet alternative
claims.believers: A commenter in the same thread suggests castor oil because it seems less obviously cosmetic.[3]
claims.experts: The 2011 review of lash enhancement notes that safety and efficacy of many over-the-counter lash-growth products have not been fully studied; it does not evaluate castor oil specifically.[8]

claims.claim: Mascara can pass as natural lashes on some men
claims.believers: The original poster suggests that men with thick, dark body hair might pass it off as naturally hairy.[3]
claims.experts: No published research examines how noticeable men's mascara use is to observers.

claims.claim: Mascara looks natural if it is applied lightly
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says the lower lashes made the biggest difference and that the challenge was not getting caught, and another poster asks others for opinions on photos with mascara on [3][6].
claims.experts: No published research examines how noticeable men's mascara is to observers; the 2011 lash-enhancement review addresses women's lash appearance [8].

claims.claim: Waterproof mascara carries extra chemical exposure
claims.believers: Wikipedia notes that manufacturers often do not label PFAS content, so the presence of the chemicals in long-wear products is not visible to buyers [1].
claims.experts: A 2021 survey of 231 products found organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, most often in waterproof mascara, and California and France have banned intentionally added PFAS in cosmetics [1][2].

claims.claim: Old or shared mascara can cause eye infections
claims.believers: The two-to-four-month shelf life is widely repeated in cosmetics guidance [1].
claims.experts: A randomized pilot study of 40 women tracked microbial contamination of mascara tubes used for three months, and case reports describe eye and eyelid complications; the FDA-cited shelf life is two to four months [1][7][10][11].

card.summary: A lash-darkening cosmetic with a long history; waterproof versions resist water and are harder to remove, and no research tests its looks effect.
card.note: Waterproof types ranked highest for detected organic fluorine (PFAS indicator) in a 2021 cosmetics survey.

quick.overview:
Mascara darkens, thickens and lengthens eyelashes using pigments, oils and waxes. Waterproof versions resist water and sweat and typically need an oil-based remover.

Some men in looksmaxxing forums discuss using it on the lower lashes for a more defined eye area. No clinical studies of its effect on attractiveness were found.
quick.mechanism: A pigmented coating on the lash hairs makes them look darker, thicker and longer; the effect is temporary and wears off or is washed away.
quick.risks: Reported problems include allergic reactions, eyelid swelling, styes and microbial contamination of old product. A 2021 study found organic fluorine, a PFAS marker, most often in waterproof mascara.

angle.text: Mascara coats the lashes so they contrast more with the skin and eye, which can make the eye area look more defined. Some men apply it sparingly to the lower lashes; waterproof formulas are chosen where sweat or water would smudge a standard product.
